What is Liquidation Cascade?

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date.

DETAILED DEFINITION

In a leveraged market, falling collateral value or adverse price changes can cause positions to breach maintenance requirements. Forced reductions may add buying or selling pressure. If that pressure worsens prices for other leveraged positions, additional liquidations can follow. Such feedback can occur in either direction and does not require a universal leverage ratio or loss threshold. Actual liquidation terms depend on the instrument, collateral, mark-price method, maintenance tiers and venue procedures. A price wick alone does not measure the amount liquidated or identify its cause. TradeHQ does not provide leveraged positions or a liquidation engine; examples remain separate arithmetic exercises.

HOW IT WORKS

A liquidation cascade is feedback in which forced position reductions add price pressure that can trigger further reductions. Venue rules, collateral and liquidity affect the outcome.

KEY POINTS
Feedback depends on leverage, collateral rules and available liquidity
Forced reductions can amplify an adverse move; totals require event-specific evidence
Often creates wicking patterns on candlestick charts
💡 WHY THIS MATTERS

Compare a hypothetical price shock with documented margin rules. A cascade label does not establish exact liquidation levels. TradeHQ does not implement leveraged positions or margin calls.

Worked exercise and its limits

A hypothetical $1,000 collateral amount supports $10,000 exposure. A 5% adverse price change creates a $500 loss before costs. Actual liquidation depends on maintenance requirements and venue rules; TradeHQ does not simulate forced liquidation.

References and scope
SEC Investor.gov — leveraged investing risks
